title: The Names, the Fall, and the comprehensive Muhammadan reality
matn:
The Infinite excludes no possibility, and creation unfolds the possibilities of manifestation without adding to God's perfection. The cosmos discloses the divine Names through distinct beings and relations; the complete human gathers their meanings in knowledge and character. God forms and teaches Ādam for this comprehensive vocation. As His *khalīfa*, the human being recognizes creation's dependence upon its Source and enacts the rightful relations among its goods.

The Garden presents human life in its original harmony, with created things open to their higher meanings. The loss of that harmony begins when a sign no longer directs the soul beyond itself. Satan promises Ādam and his spouse immortality through the forbidden tree, attaching a longing for the Eternal to a finite means against God's command. They eat and acknowledge their wrong; God accepts Ādam's repentance and gives guidance. The aspiration for permanence receives its true direction through remembrance and obedience. The descent fulfils the earthly vocation God had announced before the lapse.

Iblīs makes his limited perception sovereign. He judges Ādam by clay, claims superiority through fire and persists against the command. His judgment encloses the human being within one outward feature and defends the image of a superior servant. Even devotion becomes a veil when the lover makes his chosen relation to the Beloved the condition of obedience. Divine wisdom encompasses this rebellion and brings opportunities for resistance, discernment and repentance through the trial. The tempter seeks another's ruin while the penitent receives the grace of returning to God.

Earthly life requires provision through successive causes, cooperation among persons and the formation of capacities through repeated action. Labour, craftsmanship and the diversity of human desires supply the means of responsible earthly life. Disorder arises when a particular good displaces its proper end: remembrance becomes unquestioning allegiance, provision becomes hoarding, authority becomes domination, and knowledge becomes self-exaltation. Revelation restores judgment; worship and virtue join understanding, desire and action. Return restores human integrity and opens beyond separate individuality toward God.

The prophets address these possibilities under different conditions. Nūḥ builds the Ark under revelation; at the flood he calls his son aboard and receives divine instruction concerning the promised household. Hūd challenges the pretence of permanence in monumental power, and Shuʿayb restores exchange to truthful measure. Ibrāhīm rejects the divinization of created forms and establishes a sanctuary where household, pilgrimage, security and livelihood serve worship. Yūsuf interprets concealed meanings, preserves fidelity through temptation and confinement, and turns foresight into provision across years of abundance and scarcity. Mūsā confronts oppressive sovereignty, leads Israel from bondage and forms outward freedom through covenant and law.

Dāwūd joins praise, craftsmanship and just judgment; Sulaymān exercises wide dominion as a received trust. Their authority orders earthly life through knowledge of its ultimate Source. ʿĪsā's extraordinary signs of life disclose divine agency through a created messenger and direct the witnesses toward their Lord. These missions reveal different dimensions of human perfection within the common summons to God.

Muḥammad ﷺ completes their succession through the final revelation, whose address reaches people and generations beyond its original recipients. The Qurʾān confirms and governs the reception of earlier guidance; the Prophet's life joins knowledge, worship, inward purification, household relationships and public responsibility. Ibrāhīm's House becomes the common orientation of believers across the earth. The final dispensation gathers the forms of good under a guidance enacted among different persons and circumstances. Its enduring principles form the capacities of the individual, order household and communal relationships, and orient public judgment. Fiqh gives determinate normative expression to aspects of these acts; ethical and spiritual formation cultivate the responsible agent; practical governance applies knowledge to changing forms of common life. Prophecy ends; humanity inherits the work of understanding, embodying and transmitting its guidance.
sharh:
Divine plenitude and the human vocation

The Infinite excludes no possibility; manifestation unfolds the possibilities whose nature admits manifestation. It adds nothing to God’s knowledge or perfection. Creation possesses a real yet dependent existence, sustained at every moment by its uncreated Source. The divine Names express the relations through which one Source sustains diverse beings. Life, knowledge, power and beauty appear in creatures according to their capacities as expressions of one undivided Source.[^n1]

The world distributes these possibilities; human nature gathers them. The body belongs to the material order, sensation encounters particular things, imagination presents forms beyond immediate perception, intellect apprehends meanings, and will directs action. The heart can recognize the divine significance of the whole. Teaching Ādam the names joins this receptive constitution to knowledge of what it can apprehend. Humanity knows the things it names and can discern their relations, powers and corresponding responsibilities.[^n2]

**Comprehensiveness orders knowledge, faculties and action toward their appropriate ends.** Knowledge ordered by humility serves truth; mercy informed by judgment protects rightful claims; just judgment governed by compassion recognizes the actual persons involved. Perfection gives each capacity its proper scope. Its perfection preserves the rightful distinction and cooperation of the faculties.

*Khilāfa* turns this comprehensiveness into responsibility. A vicegerent receives the goods he must protect and the authority by which he acts. Provision, teaching, craftsmanship and judgment serve different needs within one vocation. Knowing their Source prevents delegated power from becoming a claim of independent sovereignty. Such knowledge directs the acquisition and right exercise of the technical competence appropriate to each responsibility.[^n3]

The Garden and the loss of inward vision

Paradisal integrity joins the enjoyment of creatures to recognition of their Source. The world nourishes the body while its appearances disclose spiritual meanings. Human perfection orders the faculties around spiritual knowledge; transcendent realization passes beyond confinement within separate individuality. These degrees concern the depth of realization and the soul's relation to its end.[^n4]

Harmony can nevertheless persist as an inheritance after its inward principle is no longer directly realized. Conduct, custom and received forms can preserve a good order even when their possessors understand its grounds only imperfectly. Their goodness remains real, but a plausible alternative can displace them because recognition no longer sustains conformity from within. The inward history of the Fall passes from direct vision through inherited harmony to disordered desire. The primordial human couple act and return together: their temptation addresses a shared longing, both acknowledge wrongdoing, and the promise of divine guidance opens their earthly vocation. This spiritual sequence interprets states of humanity; its relation to the historical Ādam's individual life is treated separately in the textual apparatus.[^n4]

Satan addresses the longing for permanence, promising immortality through a forbidden tree. The aspiration exceeds ordinary appetite: the soul seeks abiding life beyond the reach of decay. The deception substitutes possession of a created object for dependence upon the Eternal. A sign becomes a veil when its appearance absorbs the attention it should direct beyond itself. The supposed power of the tree belongs to the tempter's promise, which directs the longing for permanence toward created possession.

Ādam and his spouse already dwell together when they receive the prohibition. Both eat and acknowledge wrongdoing; God accepts Ādam’s repentance and grants guidance. The return preserves the distinction between a good aspiration and its wrongful pursuit. The earthly vocation precedes the lapse, while the descent changes the conditions under which humanity fulfils it. Repentance restores the relation to God and renews the servant's bodily responsibilities within earthly life.[^n5]

The restricted vision of Iblīs arises when a faculty suited to perceiving particular forms claims authority over a comprehensive human reality. Estimation (*wahm*) grasps individual significances; intellect and heart can relate them to more universal meanings. The comparison of fire and clay operates within a limited field of perception. When that comparison governs obedience, the restriction becomes a moral act. The body presents Ādam in a perceptible form while the human spiritual constitution gathers faculties whose unified reality becomes intelligible through divine teaching. Even considerable intellectual ability can coexist with an incapacity to receive correction when the will defends its preferred image of the self.[^n24]

Iblīs: a partial relation made absolute

Finite faculties receive a particular goodness through the realities they are constituted to apprehend. A creature realizes a particular good; privation arises where a good proper to it is absent, and moral disorder arises when its powers oppose their rightful ends. Deception therefore borrows attraction from something good—life, knowledge, security, devotion—while concealing the conditions of its right pursuit. A truthful proposition or worthy action can mislead when severed from its occasion, obligations or purpose.[^n6]

Iblīs makes a partial apprehension authoritative. He compares fire with clay, then treats that comparison as sufficient to reject God’s command. His error lies in granting his limited perception authority over the divine command. Ādam acknowledges a fault against the command; Iblīs makes his own judgment the standard by which the command must justify itself.

Even devotion can assume this form. Love may relinquish reward yet retain the identity of the exceptional lover. Rejection then confirms that identity, while correction threatens it. Fidelity becomes obstinacy when the servant will accept the Beloved only through a relation of his own choosing. The corruption occurs when the lover requires a particular relation to the Beloved in order to preserve his own chosen spiritual identity. Repentance relinquishes both the fault and the self-interpretation that protects it.[^n7]

The inward fixation also discloses the breadth of providence. A suggestion intended to ruin someone may occasion resistance, humility or repentance. The tempter’s consuming intention can prevent him from grasping this wider result. Divine wisdom encompasses Iblīs's agency and governs consequences extending beyond the tempter's knowledge and purpose. His own intention remains directed toward temptation while divine wisdom governs consequences beyond his knowledge.[^n8]

Concealment participates in a manifested order as a dependent mode through which discernment and disclosure become apparent. Beauty can organize contrast; providence can overcome an adversarial intention. The moral character of the tempter's own intention remains determined by his rejection of the divine command. The perfected servant understands opposition within providence and directs his own willing toward obedience. The whole includes what his conduct must reject.[^n9]

Labour, habit and return

Earthly life separates desire from fulfilment through distance, time and intermediate causes. Hunger calls for obtaining food through created means; a just intention calls for discovering the relevant facts. Cultivation requires seasons, tools and cooperation; judgment requires evidence, discernment and enforcement. Labour bridges a practical gap between a capacity and its achieved good. The difficulty of earthly labour discloses the human dependence through which knowledge and cooperation develop.[^n10]

Work also forms the worker. Repeated acts train perception, restrain impulse and stabilize skill. They can equally establish carelessness, domination or entitlement. A *malaka* is an acquired disposition whose moral quality depends upon what it enables its possessor to do. It becomes virtuous when it makes right action stable and responsive to circumstance. A rigid habit can preserve yesterday’s answer while losing the judgment that made it appropriate.

Desires conflict because finite persons pursue several goods through limited time and resources. Rest, nourishment, learning, companionship and service are coordinated goods in a rightly ordered life. Judgment orders their claims. Disorder begins when one demand acquires an unconditional priority: present appetite excludes future need, personal advantage excludes another’s right, or institutional survival excludes the purpose for which the institution exists.

Worship draws the faculties repeatedly toward their common end. Recitation addresses understanding; prayer joins attention to bodily action; fasting restrains appetite; giving subjects possession to responsibility. Their revealed authority and spiritual significance exceed their psychological effects, but those effects help explain how remembrance becomes a lived disposition. Repetition restores what distraction repeatedly disperses.[^n11]

Return therefore has two connected depths. Primordial integrity reunites knowledge, desire, will and action within the human state. Transcendent realization passes beyond attachment to the separate self. The first restores the full order of the human faculties; the second opens realization beyond the limits of separate individuality. Both preserve the proper objects of spiritual knowledge and particular expertise. Recognition of the ultimate end guides a continuing education in the material means required by each occupation.[^n4][^n3]

Continuity and preservation: Nūḥ

A community inherits both goods and habits of interpreting them. Ancestry carries language, affection and knowledge across generations, while fidelity to God establishes the meaning of prophetic succession. When inherited practice becomes immune to judgment, the vehicle of transmission claims the authority of what it should transmit. Historical continuity then imitates eternity: what has lasted appears entitled to last, and belonging replaces recognition.

Nūḥ’s narrative distinguishes these forms of continuity. His preaching challenges inherited worship; the Ark preserves life through a judgment that dissolves the existing order. He builds under divine instruction. Revelation supplies the direction, craftsmanship supplies the vessel, and trust refuses to mistake the vessel for an independent source of safety.

His son relies on a mountain. Elevation can protect against ordinary floodwaters; the scene of divine judgment subjects even familiar means of refuge to the revealed promise. The family's promised preservation is defined by God's address and the fidelity it requires. The story relates natural support and kinship to the higher claim of divine guidance and promise.

The Ark also signifies an integration capable of surviving dissolution. Body and spirit, sensible form and meaning, revealed law and spiritual realization are mutually ordered dimensions of human receptivity. Preservation carries living worship and responsibility through the loss of an older social order. The Flood joins judgment to a newly entrusted continuity of worship and responsibility.[^n12]

Covenant and the sacred centre: Ibrāhīm

Ibrāhīm distinguishes the Creator from the visible forms through which people seek ultimate power. Celestial brilliance discloses a created sign; its dependence directs worship toward the One who created it. His trials move recognition into action: allegiance must survive separation from customary protection and the surrender of what he loves.

The covenant gives this allegiance a durable communal form while withholding its authority from unjust descendants. The House then joins place, family, prayer, pilgrimage, security and provision. Its purpose precedes the prosperity it attracts: Ibrāhīm settles his household so that they may establish worship and asks for the livelihood that sustains it. Custodianship serves the sacred purpose entrusted to the House and its visitors.[^n13]

A sacred centre concentrates an orientation that must extend beyond the centre. Its fixed place gathers dispersed journeys; its recurring rites order time; its direction enters the worshipper’s posture. Divine appointment makes these acts religiously authoritative. Their embodied form lets an invisible end govern visible conduct. The appointed House orders human orientation through revealed worship, drawing material life toward the divine Source.

The centre also creates obligations. Pilgrims need protection and provision; residents depend upon people who come from elsewhere; sacred privilege demands service. Worship directs the end of settlement and livelihood, while provision sustains the households that enact that worship. The later corruption of sanctuary privilege concerns this relationship: benefits that sustain worship can become ends defended against worship’s demands. The Muhammadan restoration returns the House to its purpose and extends its orientation beyond the lineage that guards it.[^n14]

Interpretation becomes provision: Yūsuf

Yūsuf’s story joins symbolic knowledge, moral fidelity and administration. The opening dream discloses a destiny whose realization emerges through later events. His brothers judge through rivalry; betrayal, enslavement and prison then conceal the larger course from ordinary expectation. The narrative's completion discloses the hidden relations among its earlier events.

Interpretation moves from a presented form toward the intelligible meaning appropriate to its context. Ethical discernment makes the same crossing in action. Immediate pleasure may conceal injustice; apparent loss may preserve integrity. Yūsuf’s preference for prison over wrongdoing distinguishes the good an object promises from the consequences of obtaining it unlawfully.

In prison, interpretation accompanies the call from divided lordships to the one God. Before the king, it becomes foresight. Images of abundance and scarcity disclose successive conditions; Yūsuf converts that knowledge into cultivation, restrained consumption and storage. **Present abundance is only part of the relevant whole: future hunger has a claim upon present action.**

Knowledge must therefore govern means as well as identify ends. Grain must remain usable, labour must continue, and consumption must leave reserves. Trustworthiness protects the beneficiaries; competence makes protection effective. Either alone is insufficient. His eventual reconciliation with his brothers completes the same movement personally: power that could exact revenge instead repairs the household. Interpretation becomes practical wisdom when understanding is joined to responsible action.[^n15]

Freedom, judgment and delegated power

Mūsā confronts a king who turns entrusted power into a claim of supremacy. Pharaoh invokes his care for the child while concealing the oppression of the people. A genuine benefit becomes a false justification when detached from the wider relations in which the benefactor acts. A ruler's justice must govern the whole field of obligations, including the rights of those harmed by his administration.

Liberation from an external master opens the further work of forming desire, judgment and common life through covenant. Covenant and law direct the freedom won at the sea. A people can escape a tyrant yet remain vulnerable to fear, appetite and inherited habits of submission. Religious formation makes freedom answerable to a good beyond immediate preference.

The encounter with al-Khiḍr adds a distinction within knowledge. The visible sequence of an event gives partial access to the conditions governing its meaning. The distinction between witnessed facts and extraordinary disclosure preserves the evidentiary duties governing ordinary public judgments. It distinguishes an extraordinary disclosure from the evidence on which others must act.[^n16]

Dāwūd joins worship, craft and adjudication. Praise acknowledges the Source of power; workmanship directs material capacities toward protection; judgment subjects conflict to a standard of truth and justice. Sulaymān extends rule across a wider range of creatures while acknowledging its gift. Their kingdoms disclose the positive vocation of authority: coordinating differentiated powers toward goods no isolated agent could secure. The broad reach of rule remains exercised by a finite servant who depends upon God for life, knowledge and judgment.[^n17]

Their stories distinguish strength from sovereignty in the absolute sense. A ruler receives the authority to command under standards of truth and justice established by God. His authority remains accountable to the rights and ends it serves. Prophetic kingship unites these responsibilities within an entrusted person; later government preserves their rights through distinct, fallible offices.

Life and its divine Source: ʿĪsā

ʿĪsā’s conception, speech and healing make the gift of life exceptionally conspicuous. His signs exceed ordinary human powers, yet the repeated qualification “by God’s permission” identifies their agency. The messenger's greatness consists in the extraordinary disclosure entrusted to him by its divine Source.

The greater the sign, the greater the possibility of mistaking its received perfection for self-sufficiency. Diminishing the sign would also miss its meaning. Right recognition affirms both its excellence and its dependence. Spiritual teaching acquires authority by faithfully communicating and embodying the truth received from God.

Confirmation of the Torah and the alteration of certain prohibitions join this disclosure to an actual religious community. Spiritual renewal discerns the rightful relation of inherited guidance and the present obligations of the community. The life-giving sign and the correction of communal practice belong to one mission: restoring relations through which human beings receive and obey God.[^n18]

The Muhammadan gathering

The prophetic missions share one divine end but differ in audience, law, setting and characteristic disclosure. No prophet possesses only one virtue, and no community needs only one kind of correction. Their differences reveal distinct relations within human life: preservation through judgment, orientation through a sanctuary, interpretation through images, freedom through covenant, and authority through entrusted knowledge. Their unity lies in the right ordering of differentiated human relations toward God.

Muhammadan comprehensiveness gathers these perfections under one revealed orientation. In its metaphysical sense, the comprehensive divine Name embraces the differentiated Names manifested through the prophets. The Muhammadan reality has principial priority; the historical Prophet completes the succession. Principial priority and historical succession describe distinct orders of the Muhammadan manifestation.[^n19]

In the dispensation, comprehensiveness has definite consequences. Its address extends beyond the first people who receive it. Its finality excludes a later prophetic commission to supersede it. The Qurʾān confirms earlier guidance while providing the criterion governing its reception and practical laws. The Prophet's example integrates worship, purification, household obligation, livelihood and justice in the acts of one comprehensive human life.[^n20]

Universal guidance also requires accessible means. The earth provides places of prayer and means of purification; one sacred orientation unites worshippers across dispersed places. Stable obligations can operate across different environments. Suitability includes mercy, practicability and the ordering of obligations according to human capacities.[^n20]

The enduring recitation carries the sign beyond its first witnesses. Its meanings address new listeners; understanding grows through teaching, active attention and repeated practice. Teaching must make meaning intelligible; practice must make it operative; correction must prevent partial understanding from claiming the authority of the whole. Where direct spiritual vision is uncommon, preserved words, rites and disciplines provide means through which understanding and realization can be cultivated.[^n21]

Comprehensiveness is an ordered power of discernment applicable to new determinations of human life. It preserves the relationships through which new circumstances become answerable to enduring ends. Earlier missions fulfil their entrusted purposes; the final mission establishes a common criterion for the remaining history of prophetic inheritance.

The practical consequences of this metaphysical order belong to three interrelated scales. The formation of the individual (*tahdhīb al-akhlāq*, *tadbīr al-nafs*) concerns the governance of knowledge, desire, intention and will. Household governance (*tadbīr al-manzil*) concerns the ordered relationships of spouses, children, dependants, guests, possessions and livelihood. Political governance (*tadbīr al-madīna*, *al-siyāsa al-madaniyya*) concerns the coordination of rights, offices, common resources, protection and public judgment. These are simultaneous orders of practical intelligence exercised by complete human subjects.[^n25]

The Prophet's enacted practice gathers these orders. A prayer shortened for a crying child brings worship together with a mother's distress and the responsibility of a congregation's leader. A confession involving pregnancy and a dependent infant draws upon repentance, judicial evidence, public authority and the care owed by other people. Each encounter bears a determinate configuration of goods. Fiqh articulates the normative duties and limits governing these acts. The formation of character concerns the one who acts, the household communicates trust and obligations across generations, and political institutions sustain public responsibilities among strangers. Their appropriate integration is learned through rightful conduct, sound interpretation and the development of practical capacities.[^n26]

The final revelation supplies lasting ends, prescribed acts, binding rights and authoritative methods of judgment. The variable conditions of commerce, government, education and common life also require acquaintance with material circumstances, institutional means and the people affected. Sound practical discernment judges these particulars in light of enduring principles, using the legitimate interpretive methods appropriate to each field.[^n27]

From prophetic integration to historical inheritance

Finality changes the form of continuity. Prophets no longer succeed prophets, but teaching, judgment, public authority and spiritual formation must continue. These functions pass through different people, practices and institutions. The prophetic vocation is inherited through different legitimate offices, capacities and modes of spiritual realization.[^n22]

A text preserves wording; a teacher communicates understanding; repeated practice forms dispositions; a judge settles a claim; a household sustains mutual obligations; government coordinates and protects. Their contributions depend upon one another while retaining their distinct objects and standards. Learning establishes truth within its field; justice governs rightful relationships; spiritual formation transforms the acting person; political office coordinates public obligations. Integration requires both cooperation and limits.

Institutions make commitments effective beyond a single moment. Stored grain gives future hunger a claim upon present abundance. A teaching tradition allows later learners to receive knowledge from people they never meet. An endowment can sustain a purpose beyond its founder’s life. Each arrangement extends memory, responsibility and the availability of goods beyond the resources of any one person. Each can also mistake its own survival, prestige or possessions for the good it exists to serve.

The relation between soul and society is reciprocal. Persons establish practices through judgment and desire; established practices then train the attention, habits and expectations of later persons. A private distortion can acquire public durability, while a well-ordered practice can educate those still learning its underlying purpose. Renewal requires the appropriate conjunction of formed character, credible institutions and sound public judgment. Renewal restores the relation between persons, practices and ends.

**Ādam receives a comprehensive vocation; the prophets disclose its realization under differing conditions; Muḥammad ﷺ establishes its final revealed guidance; later communities must preserve that guidance through differentiated forms of life.** Their responsibility is to keep means answerable to enduring ends and inherited authority open to correction by truth.[^n23]

footnotes.text: **Manifestation.** René Guénon, *The Multiple States of the Being*, ch. XVII; Frithjof Schuon, *Survey of Metaphysics and Esoterism*, “Summary of Integral Metaphysics,” pp. 15–18. This opening adopts their metaphysical framework; it is not a consensus formulation of all schools of Islamic theology. “All possibility” does not mean that every possibility manifests in this world or that non-manifestation becomes manifestation.

**Constitution and names.** Qurʾān 2:30–33; Ibn ʿArabī, *Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam*, Adamic chapter; al-Jāmī, *Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam*, p. 509, on the realities deposited in human nature. This is the Akbarian interpretation of comprehensiveness, not the sole literal interpretation of the Qurʾānic names. [Arabic text](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9640/509?lang=ar).

**Comprehensiveness and expertise.** *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2361 distinguishes a conjecture about cultivation from communication on God’s authority. The examples of coordinated competences are explanatory applications, not claims that a spiritual rank automatically confers technical expertise. [Report](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2361).

**Integrity and realization.** Martin Lings, *The Book of Certainty*, chs. III–VI, especially pp. 29–33 and 40–42. His collective-symbolic reading distinguishes direct vision, inherited harmony and the loss of integrity. These are not established dates in Ādam’s individual biography; primordial and transcendent realization remain distinct.

**The narrated lapse.** Qurʾān 2:30–38; 7:19–23; 20:115–123. Al-Ālūsī, *Rūḥ al-maʿānī*, 20:121, surveys the timing of prophetic appointment and the possibilities of inadvertence or interpretation. The commentary does not decide that dispute by treating Lings’s collective symbolism as personal chronology. [Arabic commentary](https://quran-tafsir.net/alusy/sura20-aya121.html).

**Privation and apparent goods.** Schuon, *Survey*, pp. 16–18; Ibn ʿArabī, *al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya*, I:283, explains how an apparently superior act can divert someone from an established commitment. The distinction between finite limitation, privation and moral misuse organizes the synthesis. [Arabic text](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/2680/283?lang=ar).

**Devotion and fixation.** Al-Ḥallāj, *Ṭawāsīn*, “Ṭā-Sīn al-azal wa’l-iltibās,” §§3–11; Aḥmad al-Ghazālī, *Sawāniḥ*, ch. 66, trans. Nasrollah Pourjavady, p. 75. The proposed self-confirming attachment synthesizes these differing texts; neither supplies a medical diagnosis or an agreed classification of Iblīs as a perfected saint. [Ḥallāj](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/927/51?lang=ar); [*Sawāniḥ*, PDF](https://www.ghazali.org/books/sawanih.pdf).

**Psychology and providence.** Ibn ʿArabī, *Futūḥāt*, I:362: Iblīs’s avidity blinds him to the resistance or repentance God may bring from temptation. The passage identifies this as divine *makr* against Iblīs, not a benevolent result knowingly intended by him. [Arabic text](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/2680/362?lang=ar).

**Contrast and the whole.** ʿAyn al-Quḍāt, *Tamhīdāt*, second *tamhīd*: the mole represents Muhammadan determination; Iblīs appears as the concealing tresses. Guénon, *The Symbolism of the Cross*, ch. VII, distinguishes opposition from complementarity. Neither analogy makes an evil intention ethically good. [Persian text](https://ganjoor.net/eynolghozat/tamhidat/sh3); [Guénon](https://www.index-rene-guenon.org/index.php?Lang=FR&page=65&sigle=SC).

**Earthly effort.** Qurʾān 20:117–119; al-Qurṭubī on 20:117, especially bodily hardship and provision. Labour as successive realization, and its relation to cooperation, are philosophical explanations rather than a deduction of every economic arrangement from the Fall. [Arabic commentary](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/qortobi/sura20-aya117.html).

**Practice and formation.** Qurʾān 2:183; 9:103; 20:14; 29:45. Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, *Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn*, *Kitāb riyāḍat al-nafs*, sections defining character and examining its change; Lings, *The Book of Certainty*, ch. XIV, especially pp. 83–84. The allocation of functions to practices explains their cooperation; it does not exhaust their meanings or reduce them to techniques.

**Nūḥ and preservation.** Qurʾān 11:25–48; Ibn ʿAjība, *al-Baḥr al-madīd*, II:529, *ishāra* on 11:40, pairs revealed law and spiritual reality, sensible form and meaning, body and spirit. The symbolic integration does not establish every transmitted detail of the Flood. Al-Jāmī’s *Fuṣūṣ* commentary, p. 136, retains punishment before proposing a later spiritual outcome; that disputed reading is not substituted for the narrative here. [Ibn ʿAjība](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/12715/529?lang=ar); [al-Jāmī](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9640/136?lang=ar).

**Covenant and settlement.** Qurʾān 2:124–129; 6:74–83; 14:35–41; al-Ṭabarī on 14:37 explicitly connects settlement with prayer, attraction to the sanctuary and provision. [Arabic commentary](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/tabary/sura14-aya37.html).

**Centre and dispersed orientation.** Qurʾān 2:144–150; 22:25–29; 106:1–4. Guénon, *The King of the World*, chs. II and VIII, and *The Symbolism of the Cross*, chs. III–VII, supply the comparative symbolism. Divine appointment, not geometric symbolism alone, establishes the Kaʿbah’s religious authority. The institutional argument is a synthesis.

**Yūsuf: interpretation and provision.** Qurʾān 12:4–101, particularly 12:23–40, 43–55 and 100; al-Ṭabarī on 12:47 identifies the storage instructions as counsel for the people’s welfare. The connection between present abundance and future claims explicates that policy. [Arabic commentary](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/tabary/sura12-aya47.html).

**Mūsā: freedom and knowledge.** Qurʾān 26:18–22; 28:4; 7:145; 18:60–82. Al-Ṭabarī on 7:145 explains the comprehensiveness of the tablets through the commands and prohibitions entrusted to the community. Earlier guidance must not be reduced to an exclusively outward law. [Arabic commentary](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/tabary/sura7-aya145.html).

**Prophetic kingship.** Qurʾān 27:15–44; 34:10–14; 38:17–26. Worship, craft, justice and mortality supply distinct qualifications of authority. The Queen of Sheba’s detailed case and divergent readings remain in the retained dossier; this version does not repeat it as a general example of cognitive error.

**ʿĪsā and the sign of life.** Qurʾān 3:45–50; 4:171; 5:110. These paragraphs state the Qurʾānic account and its metaphysical interpretation; they are not a substitute for historical investigation of Jewish or Christian communities.

**Principial comprehensiveness.** Al-Jāmī, *Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam*, pp. 508–509, on the Muhammadan chapter: differentiated prophetic manifestations under the comprehensive Name and the relation to Ādam’s names. Principial precedence and historical finality concern different orders. [p. 508](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9640/508?lang=ar); [p. 509](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/9640/509?lang=ar).

**Scope, criterion and accessibility.** Qurʾān 5:48; 7:157–158; 33:40; *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 523a. Al-Ṭabarī on 5:48 distinguishes shared religion from differing practical laws. The universality of address does not imply identical applications in every circumstance. [Muslim](https://sunnah.com/muslim:523a); [al-Ṭabarī](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/tabary/sura5-aya48.html).

**The transmitted sign.** *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 4981; Lings, *The Book of Certainty*, chs. IV and XIV. The historical significance of continuing access is an inference from the enduring revelation; the late-cycle account remains a spiritual interpretation, not a deduction proving finality from chronology. [Report](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4981).

**Responsibility after prophecy.** *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3455 contrasts prophetic succession among the Israelites with the absence of a prophet after Muḥammad ﷺ. The differentiation of subsequent institutional responsibilities is the commentary’s inference, not additional wording of the report. [Report](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3455).

**Historical application.** The concluding account of institutions and reciprocal formation is an analytical framework for the later chapters, not a finding that every historical institution actually fulfilled its purpose. Particular cases require their own documentary evidence. The retained 46-matn revision plan specifies those investigations.

**The perceptual restriction.** In the *Muqaddimah* of Dāwūd al-Qayṣarī, as explained in Mukhtar Hussain Ali's scholarly study (pp. 47–49), *al-wahm al-kullī* accounts for Iblīs's fixation upon the particular clay form while the complete human possesses a spiritual universality. The broader exegetical basis is the Adamic *Fuṣūṣ*, Qurʾān 7:12 and 38:76. This is later metaphysical interpretation, identified here rather than imported into the revealed wording.

**Three divisions of practical philosophy.** Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, *Akhlāq-i Nāṣirī*, treats *tahdhīb-i akhlāq*, *tadbīr-i manzil* and *siyāsat-i mudun*. Ibn Sīnā also distinguishes individual ethics, household governance and civic government. Compare Michael Marmura, “Avicenna on the Divisions of the Sciences in the Isagoge of His Shifāʾ,” and the discussion in *History of Islamic Philosophy* of Ṭūsī's practical philosophy.

**Personal, household and civic dimensions of the transmitted acts.** Al-Bukhārī 709 reports the shortened prayer and maternal distress. Muslim 1695a–b records the cases of Māʿiz and the Ghāmidī woman, with variant reports on childbirth, nursing, punishment and repentance. The philosophical tripartition provides an analytic description of the duties encountered; it is not wording attributed to the Prophet.

**Open-ended interpretation and binding legal form.** Islamic normative law includes explicit duties and prohibitions, legal determination of new cases, context-sensitive methods and public welfare under established evidentiary limits. See “Islamic Normative Legal Theory: Framework and Applications,” *Journal of Law and Religion* (Cambridge), and the earlier Sīrah source dossiers. The methods vary across schools and cases.
